title: Llama Family
name: Llama Family
description: The Llama family is Meta AI’s production-focused set of decoder-only foundation models engineered for scalable deployment across edge, server, and datacenter environments; the family includes multilingual and vision-capable variants, long-context support up to 128K tokens, and a safety-filtering variant (Llama Guard) for integrated moderation pipelines.

architecture.architecture_type: Decoder-only Transformer family; Llama 3 variants include multilingual and vision-capable extensions (vision encoder coupling for 3.2-vision) and optimizations for production inference such as GQA on specified sizes.
architecture.transformer_type: Decoder-only (autoregressive) for language models; multimodal variants pair a vision frontend with the decoder backbone for vision-language tasks.
architecture.tokenizer: Meta-reported tokenizer with a 128K vocabulary for Llama 3 line (designed for more efficient multilingual encoding)

transformers.notes: Hugging Face Transformers provides model cards and loader utilities for Llama/Code Llama and associated tokenizers; official model cards present weights and tags.

vllm.notes: vLLM supports Llama 3 family in community/official guidance for high-throughput server inference and long-context configurations; recommended for low-latency batched workloads.

sglang.notes: SGLang (and language/serving frameworks aligned with Meta guidance) community documents support for Llama 3 inference patterns; check framework docs for version specifics.

ollama.notes: Ollama community runtimes integrate Llama-family models; support depends on model artifact availability and conversion (community).

llama_cpp.notes: llama.cpp provides native C/C++ inference and GGUF support for Llama variants and is the canonical lightweight runtime for edge/CPU deployment; community provides conversion and quantized builds.

mlx.notes: MLX ecosystem supports conversions and inference adapters; community maturity varies by variant.

litellm.notes: LiteLLM-style runtimes target efficient inference for quantized Llama-family artifacts (community).

openrouter.notes: OpenRouter community routing supports exposing Llama-family models; integration depends on artifact format.

lm_studio.notes: LM Studio community tooling supports Llama-family model packaging and local deployment; suitable for developer experimentation.

tensorrt_llm.notes: TensorRT-LLM supports optimized GPU inference for large Llama variants via model conversion (NV tools); recommended for high-throughput GPU production paths.

inference_notes: Community-supported GPTQ / AWQ / INT8 pipelines are effective for reducing memory with acceptable quality trade-offs; test quantized checkpoints before production rollout as quality varies by task and quant method.
Grouped-Query Attention reduces memory and compute overhead for large heads (documented by Meta for 8B/70B) and should be leveraged by runtimes that implement GQA-aware kernels.

Long-context: 128K context requires runtime and memory engineering (KV cache windowing, FlashAttention or partitioned attention) and may need activation/memory recomputation strategies on training/serving paths.
deployment_notes: Small variants (3B/8B) are practical for single-GPU or CPU+quantized deployment; 70B requires multi-GPU with model parallelism and 405B requires datacenter sharding approaches with orchestration and cross-node KV handling.
Safety: Use Llama Guard model as an input/output safety filter to reduce unsafe outputs; integrate filters as a separate pipeline stage to maintain throughput and allow independent updates.
Checkpoints: Use base/instruct checkpoints according to downstream needs — instruct-tuned variants for chat/agent workflows, base for fine-tuning and RAG preparation.
optimization_notes: Use runtime-specific optimizations: vLLM for throughput and long-context, TensorRT-LLM for GPU-optimized kernels, and llama.cpp for edge GGUF builds.
KV cache tuning: adjust KV storage and eviction strategies for long sessions; examine runtime docs for memory vs. latency trade-offs.
compatibility_notes: Tokenizer compatibility: Ensure the 128K tokenizer/vocab is used consistently across tokenization, fine-tuning, and inference stages to avoid mis-encoding; use official tokenizer artifacts when available.
Prompt formats: Instruction-tuned variants expect specific instruction formats described in model cards — preserve prompt/response separators used during post-training.
migration_notes: From Llama 2 → Llama 3: Llama 3 introduced GQA and a larger vocabulary; check tokenizer and attention differences when migrating fine-tuned models — conversion may be non-trivial if tokenizer or architecture differs.
Fine-tuning: QLoRA and LoRA-style parameter-efficient fine-tuning are community-standard for large Llama variants; use published guidance and test on representative workloads.
common_pitfalls: Over-quantization: Aggressive quantization can degrade code generation or reasoning performance — validate on holdout tasks before production use.
Under-provisioned sharding: Deploying 70B/405B without proper interconnect and model-parallel orchestration will cause out-of-memory or performance instability — design for memory and bandwidth.
Safety latency: Running Llama Guard synchronously in the request path can add latency; prefer asynchronous or queued filter stages if low-latency is critical.

best_for: Multilingual conversational systems requiring strong language coverage and instruction following.
Long-context retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and document understanding up to 128K tokens with optimized runtimes.
On-device/edge CPU inference of small variants via llama.cpp/GGUF + quantization (3.2-3b, 3.1-8b).
avoid_for: Environments requiring strict, proprietary-hosted model SLAs where closed-source vendor-managed models are mandated.
Extremely latency-sensitive tiny microservices where model load/quantization overhead cannot be tolerated (unless using converted micro/quantized builds).
Use cases requiring published MoE or model-internal tool APIs.
engineering_snapshot.recommended_use_case: Multilingual chat and RAG with long-context needs where self-hosting, fine-tuning, and quantized inference across edge to datacenter are primary requirements.
deployment_risks: KV cache memory growth with long contexts.
Quantization quality trade-offs for edge deployment.
failure_modes: Prompt format mixing across versions can silently degrade quality; tokenizer mismatch causing malformed prompts.
Memory exhaustion (OOM) with large context windows or under-provisioned sharding.
hidden_costs: Quantization tuning and validation for production quality.
scaling_issues: Tensor parallelism and model-parallel orchestration required for 70B/405B variants.
KV cache management at scale and high concurrency.

timeline.notes: Official Meta blog and technical report release describing Llama 3 family and Llama Guard.

choose_if: You need a self-hostable, instruction-capable model family with long-context (up to 128K), multilingual coverage, and vision-language options for production deployments where control over data and fine-tuning is required.
avoid_if: You require a provider-managed hosted service with vendor SLA for model improvements and where licensing forbids local hosting; or if your team cannot manage quantization/serving complexity for >70B deployments.
watch_out_for: Large-parameter variants (70B, 405B) require multi-GPU sharding and careful KV/cache memory planning; community consensus on minimum hardware is guidance rather than official requirements — verify with runtime docs (vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, SGLang) before provisioning.
engineering_decision.best_deployment_scenario: Use Llama small/medium variants (3.2-3b, 3.1-8b) with GGUF + AWQ/INT8 quantization on edge/CPU (llama.cpp) for low-cost self-hosting; use 70B on multi-GPU server with vLLM/TensorRT-LLM for higher-quality reasoning workloads; reserve 405B for datacenter sharded deployments with high memory & orchestration investment.
